evidence.claim: The Historic Lewes Byway covers 12.35 miles on six roads, linking town streets with the Delaware Bay shore.
evidence.quote: Length 12.35 miles on Pilottown Road/First Street, Gills Neck Road, New Road, Kings Highway, Cape Henlopen Drive and Savannah Road.

evidence.quote: Drive Time 1 hour

evidence.claim: At Cape Henlopen, the Great Dune rises 80 feet above sea level, while walking dunes move slowly across pine forests.
evidence.quote: the "Great Dune" rises 80 feet above sea level is famous for its "walking dunes" that slowly move across the pine forests.

evidence.claim: Kings Highway linked Lewes at the mouth of Delaware Bay with Wilmington, its economic center.
evidence.quote: Located at the mouth of the Delaware Bay, Lewes was linked to the economic center of Wilmington by Kings Highway

evidence.claim: Harbor protection, lighthouses and the defense of the bay became part of the town’s maritime role.
evidence.quote: The importance of a good harbor and lighthouses made Lewes the perfect spot as a major shipping channel, for rescuing passengers and crews of foundering ships, and for defending the Delaware Bay and adjacent communities.

evidence.claim: In 2008, DelDOT approved the Lewes Byway as a Delaware Scenic and Historic Highway, bringing these roads into the state’s byway system.
evidence.quote: The Lewes Byway was approved as a Delaware Scenic and Historic Highway by DelDOT in 2008.

evidence.claim: Begin from the land on Kings Highway, Savannah Road or New Road.
evidence.quote: The Byway route can begin at the "Gateways from the Land" on Kings Highway, Savannah Road and New Road;

evidence.claim: In Lewes, the byway’s stops include the Zwaanendael Museum and Lightship Overfalls.

evidence.claim: A stepped gable, terra cotta roof tiles and decorated shutters give the Zwaanendael Museum its Dutch architectural vocabulary.
evidence.quote: It has 17th century Dutch elements such as stepped facade gable, terra cotta roof tiles, carved stonework, and decorated shutters.

evidence.claim: The museum was created to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Zwaanendael, Delaware’s first European settlement, founded in 1631.
evidence.quote: the Zwaanendael Museum was created to honor the 300th anniversary of Delaware's first European settlement, Zwaanendael, founded 1631.

evidence.claim: Wilmington architect E. William Martin designed the building.

evidence.claim: Its exhibits follow southeastern Delaware’s coastal history through shipwrecks such as HMS DeBraak, lighthouses and the pilots of the Delaware River and Bay.
evidence.quote: Exhibits include local history, shipwrecks such as the H.M.S. DeBraak and lighthouses, Cape Henlopen Lighthouse, the bombardment of Lewes by the British in the War of 1812, pilots of the Delaware River and Bay, and the ever-changing Delaware coastline.

evidence.claim: Above the front stands a statue of David Pietersen de Vries, one of the colony’s patroons.
evidence.quote: The  top of the building's front features a statue of David Pietersen de Vries, one of the patroons of the Swanendael colony.

evidence.claim: The name painted on Lightship Overfalls does not describe where this vessel served.
evidence.quote: painted for the "OVERFALLS" station, though she never served there.

evidence.claim: Its working stations were Cornfield Point in Connecticut, then Cross Rip and Boston in Massachusetts.
evidence.quote:
1938-1957: Cornfield Point, Connecticut
1958-1962: Cross Rip, Massachusetts
1962-1972: Boston, Massachusetts

evidence.claim: Built to replace a ship damaged in the 1938 New England hurricane, it was the last riveted-hull lightship built for the United States Lighthouse Service.
evidence.quote: She is the last riveted-hull lightship built for the United States Lighthouse Service, all subsequent ships having welded hulls.

evidence.claim: A severe storm damaged it in December 1970, leading to its decommissioning in 1972.
evidence.quote: A severe storm in December 1970 damaged the ship, leading to her decommissioning on November 7, 1972.

evidence.claim: After retirement it was donated to the Lewes Historical Society; it remains preserved in Lewes as a museum ship.
evidence.quote: Upon retirement WAL 539 was donated to the Lewes Historical Society and placed on display in Lewes, Delaware

evidence.claim: Built to replace a ship damaged in the 1938 New England hurricane

evidence.claim: In 1905, tons of brush were placed beside the tower and oil house to keep drifting sand from undermining them.
evidence.quote: In 1905, several tons of brush were placed about the tower and oil house to prevent the foundations and brick walls from being undermined by the drifting away of the sand.

evidence.claim: A storm undermined the tower in April 1926, and it fell seaward.

evidence.claim: Other coastal defenses survive: the Army built Fort Miles here during World War II, and concrete observation towers, bunkers and a pier remain in the park.
evidence.quote: During World War II, the U.S. Army built Fort Miles at Cape Henlopen. Numerous bunkers, concrete observation towers and the pier built to accommodate the laying of mines on the harbor floor remain today.
